evaluation.positioning_hook: After a high-school prank turns deadly, a party-loving teen and her fractured friend group are hunted by a killer who knows their secrets and keeps turning their own social chaos against them.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The slasher engine is instantly legible and the teen-friend-group setup gives it a clear audience, but the appeal is narrower than a clean commercial horror premise because the script leans heavily on melodrama and long dialogue scenes between kills. The core promise is there, but it isn’t yet packaged with the kind of sharp, singular hook that broadens beyond horror fans.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise is easy to explain once Katie’s murder and the friend-group fallout are established: a circle of teens is picked off while the group’s past prank comes back to haunt them. The issue is that the script takes a long time to settle on its true engine, with multiple false starts around Katie, Lucy, and the grandma before the Ryan reveal lands.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Sammy, Faye, Lucy, Austin, and Lauren all have strong behavioral signatures, which gives the ensemble some immediate texture. But the characters are written more as loud social types than as psychologically layered leads, so the emotional durability is limited even when the banter is lively.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script has bold volume and a willingness to go extreme, but much of the execution plays like a familiar teen-slasher with heightened soap-opera dialogue. The killer reveal and prank-backstory framework are serviceable rather than fresh, and the voice is more maximal than distinctive.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The murder set pieces and interrogation beats keep the story moving, and the body count gives the script a built-in forward drive. But the middle stretches are dominated by repetitive relationship talk and extended social scenes, which soften the urgency between attacks.

resonant_originality.reasoning: There is a usable core idea in the way a school prank metastasizes into a revenge-killer scenario, but the reveal mechanics and character dynamics are familiar horror territory. The script’s most memorable element is its intensity, not a truly surprising premise.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The high-school ecosystem, party culture, parent dynamics, and police involvement create a usable social world with enough recurring relationships to generate scenes. Still, the world mostly functions as a container for the killings and arguments rather than a deeply specific system with its own rules and pressures.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a very loud, teen-soap register, but the tone is unstable: comedy, melodrama, romance, and gore are all present, often in the same stretch. That volatility gives it personality, but not yet a controlled tonal identity.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: The Lucy insecurity thread, the Sammy-grandma trauma, and the friend-group betrayals suggest more emotional material underneath the slasher surface. The problem is that the script states those wounds directly rather than letting them accumulate with much subtext, so the depth is more declared than felt.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: This is the script’s strongest structural asset: the friend group is constantly generating friction, flirtation, jealousy, and loyalty tests, which keeps the ensemble active. Even when the dialogue is overextended, the relationships are doing real work and give the story a recurring engine beyond the killer.

lead_characters.name: Sammy Miller
lead_characters.demographics: female, 18, high-school senior, socially volatile, party-going teen
lead_characters.hook: The story’s center of gravity: loud, defensive, funny, and emotionally evasive, Sammy is the friend-group catalyst who keeps trying to outrun guilt, grief, and the shadow of her grandmother’s violence. She wants control, loyalty, and the freedom to keep living loudly, but her own history keeps dragging the past back into the room.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a young lead in a scream-queen lane — the kind of role that lets an actor swing from comic bravado to raw panic to moral ugliness in the same movie. It gives the performer a full-body survival arc plus the chance to own the final stretch of a body-count thriller.

lead_characters.name: Faye Woodbridge
lead_characters.demographics: female, 18, high-school senior, talkative, emotionally intense
lead_characters.hook: Faye is the script’s loudest pressure valve: oversharing, needy, romantic, and constantly trying to keep the group together even as she burns people out. Under the chatter is a real fear of abandonment, which makes her grief and panic feel personal when the killings start.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the same volatile, scene-stealing runway as a high-energy supporting turn in a teen ensemble horror film — big laughs, big tears, and a hard pivot into terror. It’s a showcase for comic timing, emotional speed, and physical panic.

lead_characters.name: Lucy Carmen
lead_characters.demographics: female, 17, high-school junior, withdrawn, insecure, socially isolated
lead_characters.hook: Lucy is the quiet fracture in the group: observant, wounded, and desperate to be chosen, then suddenly cruel when she feels invisible. Her arc is built on shame, self-image, and the need to matter, which makes her both sympathetic and volatile.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong material for an actor who can play repression turning into eruption — the kind of performance territory that rewards stillness, then pays off with a late emotional confession. It gives the performer a dark, wounded arc inside an ensemble horror structure.

lead_characters.name: Austin Moore
lead_characters.demographics: male, 18, high-school senior, popular, college-bound, confident
lead_characters.hook: Austin is the polished social operator of the group: charming, competitive, image-conscious, and always trying to manage the room. He reads like the guy who can talk his way through anything until the pressure finally exposes how self-serving he can be.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor play charisma as a weapon, then let the mask slip under pressure. It’s a good showcase for a young leading-man type who can do swagger, jealousy, and panic without losing audience interest.

lead_characters.name: Lauren Cheng
lead_characters.demographics: female, 17, high-school junior, observant, romantic, emotionally steady
lead_characters.hook: Lauren is the calmer counterweight in the group, but she’s not passive; she watches, processes, and quietly steers the emotional temperature of the room. Her loyalty is real, but so is her insecurity, especially once the Austin-Julia-Lauren triangle starts to crack.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that benefits an actor who can play intelligence without showboating — the grounded friend who becomes the emotional barometer of the ensemble. It’s a strong support turn with romance, hurt, and moral clarity.

lead_characters.name: Daniel Stokes-Simpson
lead_characters.demographics: male, 18, high-school senior, athlete, boyfriend, socially smooth
lead_characters.hook: Daniel is the easygoing popular guy who smooths over conflict, jokes through tension, and keeps the group moving until the script needs him to become a victim. He functions as both social glue and a pressure-release valve for Faye’s intensity.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a classic teen-horror boyfriend role with enough banter to give an actor charm before the kill sequence turns it into a physical showcase. It’s the kind of part that can make a young actor memorable fast.

lead_characters.name: Eric Smith
lead_characters.demographics: male, 17, high-school junior, quiet, socially withdrawn, new kid energy
lead_characters.hook: Eric is the soft-spoken outsider who keeps getting pulled into the group’s emotional weather without ever fully owning the room. His silence reads as mystery, insecurity, and restraint, which makes him useful both as a romantic object and as a late-story victim.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor a quiet, watchful presence in an ensemble and then a sudden horror payoff. It’s good material for someone who can play interiority and vulnerability without needing speeches.

lead_characters.name: Ryan
lead_characters.demographics: male, late teens, high-school age, outsider, deceptive, physically dangerous
lead_characters.hook: Ryan is the late-arriving emotional trap: initially awkward and sympathetic, then revealed as the manipulative engine behind the killings. He weaponizes intimacy, grievance, and false vulnerability, which makes him the script’s clearest antagonist.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of reveal role that lets an actor play two tracks at once — wounded outsider and hidden predator — which is catnip for a young villain turn. It gives the performer a big late-game switch and a final confrontation payoff.

lead_characters.name: Officer Wilson
lead_characters.hook: Officer Wilson is the procedural pressure point: skeptical, blunt, and increasingly entangled because his son is part of the friend group. He gives the script a law-enforcement frame and a family complication at the same time.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is solid character-actor territory — a role that lets an actor play authority, irritation, and paternal conflict in the same scenes. It’s especially useful because the son/father dynamic gives the part a personal edge.

lead_characters.name: Katie Davis
lead_characters.hook: Katie is the absent catalyst whose death and bullying history drive the entire plot. She exists mostly as a memory, accusation, and moral stain on the friend group.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is not a performance-heavy role, but it is structurally important as the emotional and narrative trigger. It’s the kind of part that matters more as a plot engine than as a showcase.

notable_requirements: multiple teen bedrooms and family homes

technical.vfx_details: primarily blood, wound, and kill-enhancement work; no major creature or environment effects
technical.sfx_needs: practical knife work, gunshot effects, blood rigs, body bags, and repeated gore makeup

rights_flags.detail: Get Out is specifically named as a movie the characters watch.
McDonald’s is specifically named in dialogue.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: genre-forward streaming or specialty theatrical with a strong horror audience

budget.note: Contemporary teen settings keep the footprint manageable, but the repeated murder sequences, blood effects, night work, and multiple house interiors will push above a lean contained-thriller cost profile.

casting.note: The project needs a large ensemble of age-specific teen roles with distinct comic and emotional rhythms, plus a villain reveal that has to land after playing sympathetic for much of the script.

development.note: The script’s biggest friction is structural clarity: the killer identity, motive chain, and friend-group blame logic shift repeatedly, so the buyer conversation will center on whether the narrative spine feels locked.

comp_set.title: Scream
comp_set.why_it_comps: Teen ensemble slasher dynamics, friend-group suspicion, and a killer who turns social history into murder fuel.

comp_set.title: I Know What You Did Last Summer
comp_set.why_it_comps: A past wrongdoing comes back as a body-count engine, with teen relationships and guilt driving the suspense.

comp_set.title: Bodies Bodies Bodies
comp_set.why_it_comps: A young ensemble trapped in escalating paranoia, with relationship chaos and accusation as part of the horror engine.

comp_set.title: Fear Street Part One: 1994
comp_set.why_it_comps: Streaming-friendly teen horror with a group dynamic, stylized kills, and a mystery tied to past violence.

audience_target.primary_audience: Horror fans who like teen ensembles, relationship drama, and a high body count with emotional betrayals.
audience_target.demographics: Primarily 16-34, skewing female but with broad teen-horror crossover; strongest with genre viewers who like group dynamics and messy romance.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary locations and limited effects keep it in indie horror territory, though the repeated kill scenes and ensemble cast prevent it from being ultra-lean.

types_of_buyers: indie producers in the elevated-teen-horror lane
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the teen-horror lane where ensemble chemistry, body count, and a clean revenge engine matter more than star power. The script’s contemporary setting and contained locations make it a practical genre buy if the killer reveal is tightened.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature with no clear sequel or universe vector beyond the central revenge story.

strengths.what_it_means: That gives the movie a repeatable scene engine and a clear reason for buyers to see a cast-driven horror package rather than a one-note slasher. It will appeal to producers looking for a young ensemble that can play banter, betrayal, and panic in the same movie.
strengths.evidence: The cafeteria and party scenes keep rotating alliances, crushes, and resentments, especially around Sammy, Faye, Austin, Lauren, Lucy, and Eric.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The script has a built-in revenge spine.
strengths.what_it_means: A past prank turning into a murder spree is a clean commercial engine because it gives the killings a motive the audience can track. That makes the project legible to horror buyers who want a simple hook with escalating consequences.
strengths.evidence: Katie’s bullying/prank history is repeatedly referenced, then folded into the killer’s revenge logic and the police interrogations.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Faye is a scene-stealing pressure valve.
strengths.what_it_means: Her volume, insecurity, and emotional overdrive create a memorable supporting role that can pop in casting conversations. Buyers often respond to a character who can deliver both comic relief and genuine panic, and Faye does that repeatedly.
strengths.evidence: Her long cafeteria monologues, her panic after Daniel dies, and her frantic survival run give her a very specific performance lane.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The kill sequences are frequent and clear.
strengths.what_it_means: That keeps the movie in a commercially familiar horror lane and gives the trailer team obvious set pieces to cut around. Genre audiences know exactly what kind of ride they’re buying.
strengths.evidence: Katie, Julia, Daniel, Austin, Eric, Lucy, and Ryan all get explicit attack sequences with escalating gore.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The teen social world is active.
strengths.what_it_means: The script has enough relationship churn to support marketing around romance, jealousy, and betrayal rather than just murder. That broadens the emotional entry point for younger viewers who come for the social drama as much as the slasher mechanics.
strengths.evidence: The Austin/Lauren/Julia triangle, Sammy/Lucy fallout, and Faye/Daniel pairing all drive scenes before and after the attacks.

whats_special.headline: This is a castable, contemporary teen-slasher package with a clear revenge engine and enough relationship chaos to keep the ensemble alive between kills. If the killer spine is sharpened, it has a real lane as a streamer-friendly indie horror buy with trailer-ready set pieces and a few breakout supporting roles.

items.area: The killer logic shifts too often.
items.detail: The script moves from Sammy’s grandma to Lucy’s apparent breakdown to Ryan’s reveal, with the motive chain changing as the story goes. That creates real development friction because the audience is asked to reorient the mystery multiple times before the final answer lands.

items.area: The dialogue runs long between attacks.
items.detail: Several cafeteria, party, and relationship scenes stretch far past the amount of information they need to carry, especially the Faye/Austin/Lauren/Sammy exchanges. That softens momentum in a genre piece where buyers will expect the next scare or reveal to arrive faster.

items.area: The tone swings from camp to gore without control.
items.detail: The script jumps from joke-heavy teen banter to explicit mutilation and back again, often in the same sequence. That volatility gives it energy, but it also makes the lane harder to sell because the movie is not consistently one thing.

items.area: The ensemble is vivid but not equally deep.
items.detail: Sammy, Faye, Lucy, Austin, and Lauren all have strong behavioral signatures, but many supporting players function as loud types rather than fully differentiated dramatic engines. That limits long-tail attachment unless the buyer is specifically responding to the group dynamic.

items.area: The gore level narrows the buyer pool.
items.detail: The repeated throat-slits, stabbings, decapitation imagery, and prolonged attack beats push the movie firmly into mature horror territory. That is fine for streaming and genre buyers, but it will not travel as broadly as a softer teen thriller.

issues.headline: The main friction is structural, not conceptual: the script has a usable slasher engine, but the killer reveal path and motive chain keep changing, and the dialogue-heavy middle sections slow the charge between set pieces. It’s sellable as a teen-horror package, but the buyer conversation will focus on clarity, tone control, and whether the ensemble can justify the runtime.
